content.text:
## Setting up the physics

Molten-salt TES stores energy as sensible heat: E = m·Cp·ΔT. For solar salt (60% NaNO₃/40% KNO₃, the standard CSP medium), Cp ≈ 1.5 kJ/kg·K and the usable ΔT between cold (~290°C) and hot (~565°C) tanks is ~250 K. That's an energy density of **~104 Wh/kg** — roughly 1.5–2 orders of magnitude worse than Li-ion cells (~250 Wh/kg), which is the first clue that this technology wins on cost-per-kWh, not mass or volume efficiency.

For 5 MWh (5,000 kWh = 18,000 MJ):

**m = 18,000,000 kJ / (1.5 × 250) ≈ 48,000 kg (48 t) of salt**

At molten density ~1,900 kg/m³, that's ~25 m³ of salt — and since a two-tank system needs each tank sized for the *full* inventory (all salt sits in the hot tank when charged, all in the cold tank when discharged), you need two ~25–30 m³ vessels.

## Bottom-up cost build

| Component | Basis | Low ($) | High ($) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Salt (48 t) | $900–1,200/t | 43,000 | 58,000 |
| Hot + cold tanks (2× ~30 m³, SS/refractory lined, foundation heat-trace) | small-vessel fab, no scale economy | 160,000 | 300,000 |
| Charge/discharge heat exchanger(s) (~1 MWt duty) | | 50,000 | 100,000 |
| Hot salt pump(s) (specialty materials) | | 30,000 | 60,000 |
| Piping, valves, trace heating | | 40,000 | 80,000 |
| I&C | | 20,000 | 40,000 |
| Electrical, foundations, structural | | 50,000 | 100,000 |
| **Direct equipment subtotal** | | **393,000** | **738,000** |
| EPC, engineering, PM, contingency (+30–50%, heavier at small scale) | | +120,000 | +370,000 |
| **Installed total** | | **~511,000** | **~1,108,000** |

**→ $100–220/kWh installed, point estimate ~$150–160/kWh.**

This matches the known pattern from CSP literature: utility-scale 2-tank molten-salt TES (hundreds–thousands of MWh) runs ~$15–30/kWh installed, but at 5 MWh the fixed costs (foundation heating, pumps, HX, controls, EPC minimums) don't shrink proportionally, so unit cost is 5–10× higher. This is the dominant reason thermal storage doesn't show up at small scale commercially — the technology's advantage is specifically in the *marginal* cost of adding duration (more tank volume, more salt), not in small fixed-size deployments.

## Amortizing over cycle life

The key asymmetry vs. batteries: salt doesn't electrochemically degrade. Cycle life is set by tank/pipe corrosion and mechanical wear, not throughput — typically rated 20–25 years, effectively unlimited cycles (daily cycling × 25 yr ≈ 9,000 cycles with no capacity fade).

**Case A — delivered as heat** (process-heat/industrial thermal battery use, no reconversion to electricity): round-trip efficiency is thermal-loss-limited only, ~90–95%.

- Capex $750k (midpoint) / 25 yr = $30,000/yr
- O&M ~1.5%/yr of capex ≈ $11,000/yr
- Annual throughput (daily cycling) = 365 × 5,000 kWh = 1.825M kWh
- **Levelized cost ≈ $0.022–0.025/kWh delivered (~$23/MWh)**

**Case B — reconverted to electricity** (true "Carnot battery," resistive charge + Rankine discharge): RTE drops to ~40–45% (heat-engine Carnot penalty), and critically you must add a power block (turbine + generator), which for even a small unit is $500–1,500/kW — often *exceeding* the TES capex itself. Levelized cost on energy terms alone becomes ~$0.05–0.06/kWh-electric before counting the power block; including it, total system capex roughly doubles.

## Is it competitive with Li-ion?

Li-ion at this scale: installed cost ~$150–250/kWh (similar fixed-cost penalty at small size as salt TES), cycle life ~4,000–6,000 cycles / ~15 yr, RTE ~90–95%. Levelized: ~$1M capex / (5,000 cycles × 5,000 kWh) ≈ $0.04/kWh + O&M ≈ **$0.045–0.05/kWh (~$45–50/MWh)**.

**Conclusion:**

- **As heat storage**, molten salt is cheaper than Li-ion on a levelized $/kWh-delivered basis (~$20–25/MWh vs ~$45–50/MWh) — because its storage medium doesn't degrade, so a long calendar life + high cycling frequency amortizes the (higher, at this scale) upfront capex into near-nothing. This is the real use case for "thermal batteries" (Rondo, Antora, Fourth Power, etc., though those mostly use cheaper solid media like firebrick rather than molten salt specifically).
- **As a direct electricity-in/electricity-out substitute for Li-ion**, it is *not* competitive at 5 MWh: the installed $/kWh is already higher than Li-ion at this small scale (fixed-cost penalty cuts both ways), and forcing reconversion through a heat engine adds a large power-block capex plus a ~40–60% RTE penalty that Li-ion simply doesn't pay.
- Thermal storage's crossover point against Li-ion is **duration and scale**, not this comparison: it wins when you need many hours-to-days of storage at large absolute capacity (energy-dominated cost structure), where the cheap $/kWh-marginal of salt+tank beats Li-ion's roughly flat $/kWh regardless of duration. A 5 MWh / few-hour system is squarely in Li-ion's territory.
